extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishers of children's and YA books (and people working as sensitivity readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for when and how to hire and work with sensitivity readers to ensure authentic, non-harmful representation in children’s and YA manuscripts; covers roles, timing, deliverables, limits, and selection. Focuses on editorial practice within the publishing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise / lived-experience alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers are experts in a specific identity, usually the same as the characters they're assessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select readers whose lived experience aligns with the identity being portrayed (e.g., disability, race, neurodivergence). The article emphasizes that lived experience supplements research and can catch things research alone misses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role is advisory, not authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers provide feedback and flag issues but do not make changes to the manuscript or decide whether a book is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and editors retain final decision-making power. Sensitivity readers are part of the editorial process to improve a manuscript, not gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverables: in-text comments plus an editorial letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sensitivity reads consist of detailed in-text comments and an in-depth editorial letter that links to outside sources and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect both line-level suggestions and a summary letter with references; this is the common format described by professional sensitivity-read services and editors interviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: bring readers early or during major edits
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal time to engage a sensitivity reader is early (even during concept/idea stage) or alongside the editor's major round of edits; the wrong time is at the galley/last-minute stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early engagement allows for substantive revision; for minor characters or small items the read can be later, but plan ahead if extensive edits may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: flag harmful stereotyping and inauthentic portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers are hired to identify harmful or stereotyped portrayals and to ensure more authentic representation of marginalized identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article cites historical and recent examples (racist portrayals in Dr. Dolittle and Dr. Seuss; ableism in The Secret Garden; controversies like A Birthday Cake for George Washington and American Dirt) to show the kinds of harms readers aim to prevent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness for authors writing outside their experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity reads are especially valuable when authors write characters outside their own lived experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should do research but also hire readers to 'double check' aspects only lived experience reliably reveals; this is described as analogous to hiring a subject-matter expert for technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value even when author shares identity (second-opinion principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even authors who share the character's identity can benefit from sensitivity readers to gain additional perspectives and nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiences exist on a spectrum; a second set of eyes can reveal blind spots. Examples: neurodivergent author Jen Malia and sensitivity reader input improving her book; Andrew Sass's experience as a reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection / sourcing of appropriate readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers may be suggested by publishers or found by authors via communities (e.g., bookstagram); publishers may not have experts for very specific conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a publisher lacks a reader for a specific identity (e.g., sickle cell), authors can find readers through community networks. Vet readers for appropriate lived experience and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial-team diversity as a complementary safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-diverse editorial team may inadvertently overlook authentic- representation issues; team diversity reduces missed issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no one on the editorial team shares the marginalized identity in question, it's harder to spot problems—sensitivity readers should complement, not replace, diverse staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, terminology, and nuance guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers provide specific guidance on language choices, terminology, and nuanced representation (e.g., distinctions between trans and nonbinary perspectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They can influence word choice and phrasing, as in the cited example where readers helped shape language in a book about puberty; they may also link to resources to support recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research component of the read
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers often conduct research in order to provide detailed feedback and to cite sources that support their recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect references and linked resources in editorial letters; readers may back up suggestions with context, historical background, or current community practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation management: not a guarantee but increases likelihood of accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Having sensitivity readers makes it more likely a manuscript 'gets it right' but does not guarantee perfect representation or eliminate all risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/editors should understand readers reduce risk and improve authenticity, but mistakes and disagreements can still occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process variations: who initiates the read
rubrics_metrics.description: The process can be initiated by authors requesting a reader, by editors/publishers hiring one, and sometimes readers are hired without the author's knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different workflows exist; authors requesting reads can choose who to hire, while publisher-initiated reads may be handled through editorial channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: one reader does not represent an entire group
rubrics_metrics.description: No single sensitivity reader can represent the totality of experiences within a community; feedback may conflict with an author's own lived experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat readers' feedback as informed perspective rather than definitive truth. If feedback conflicts with an author's lived experience, authors can and should discuss and defend editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and practical justification: real-world impacts of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic representation matters because misrepresentation can have concrete negative effects on groups' lives (e.g., fostering myths that affect service access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives the example of the lip-reading trope leading hearing people to refuse ASL interpreters in critical situations; this explains why sensitivity reading is important beyond avoiding scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and relationship guidance: collaborative, improvement-oriented approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers are presented as allies who love books and want to help authors improve—not as antagonists or censors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach the process as collaborative; sensitivity readers' role is to help writers craft better, less harmful stories rather than to 'police' creativity.
